title: The dwelling (Exodus 35–40)
hook: everyone brings something, and the cloud fills the tent

segments.voice: Yesterday, God's back: Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing the glory only as it passed. Your line was seen from behind. What good did you notice, looking back? Day three hundred eighty-one.

Here's a sentence you will almost never hear in a parish bulletin: please stop giving, we have too much. It's in Exodus. Moses asks the people to bring materials for a tent where God will dwell among them, and he asks only for what each one's heart moves them to give. And they come, morning after morning, carrying gold jewelry, colored yarn, goat hair, wood, oil, spices. The craftsmen finally go to Moses and say: the people are bringing much more than we need. So Moses sends word through the camp: nobody make anything else for the sanctuary. The people had to be held back from giving.
screen: `FOR WHOEVER'S HEART IS MOVED.` → `MORNING AFTER MORNING.` → `PLEASE STOP. WE HAVE TOO MUCH.`

segments.voice: First, the gifts. The last six chapters of Exodus read like a building inventory, and that's the point: everyone's in it. Rulers bring precious stones. Women who are skilled spin blue and purple and scarlet yarn with their own hands, and some spin goat hair. Others bring their bronze mirrors, and those are melted down for the great washbasin. Nobody's gift is too ordinary. Second, the artist. God calls a craftsman named Bezalel and fills him with the spirit of God, in wisdom and understanding and skill, to work gold, cut stones, carve wood. He's among the first people the Bible says God filled with his Spirit, and what the Spirit gives him is talent with his hands. A partner named Oholiab works with him, and they teach others. Third, the dwelling. In Hebrew it's the mishkan, from a verb that means to dwell or to settle. It's a tent, made to be taken down and carried. When it's finished and set up, the cloud covers it, and the glory of the Lord fills it so completely that Moses himself can't go in. The God of the burning mountain now lives in a tent in the middle of the camp. Fourth, where Catholics see it every Sunday. The box on or near the altar where the Eucharist is kept is called the tabernacle, named for this tent, and the lamp burning beside it says the same thing the cloud said: God is here. John's Gospel uses the same picture: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. The Greek verb means, literally, he pitched his tent.
screen: `GOLD, YARN, GOAT HAIR, MIRRORS.` · `BEZALEL, FILLED WITH THE SPIRIT.` · `MISHKAN: THE CLOUD FILLS THE TENT.` · `THE TABERNACLE IN EVERY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one skill you could give. Settle, and breathe. Bezalel's gift was his hands. The women's gift was spinning. Somebody's gift was a mirror. What's yours? Maybe you can cook, fix a sink, keep accounts, sing, drive, sew, read aloud, set up chairs, teach a kid to read. Picture your parish, or any community you belong to, and where that gift would fit. Don't sign up for everything. Just find one place, and picture yourself bringing it. If you pray, you can offer that skill to God. If you don't, simply notice that you have something to bring. The bell holds the time.
The dwelling. The tent built from everyone's gifts, where the cloud of God's glory came to live in the middle of the camp. Today's word.
Your line: everyone brought something. Today, offer one skill to your parish or your community, even an hour, even something small. Day three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In Catholic churches the Eucharist is reserved in a tabernacle, named after the tent in Exodus, with a lamp kept burning beside it, and parishes rely on volunteers' skills, from musicians and sacristans to cooks and catechists.

fork.setup: you're one of the craftsmen. every morning the people bring more gold, yarn and wood. you already have more than the work needs. what happens?
options: you store the extra for later.
you tell Moses, and he tells the people to stop.
fork.reveal: they tell Moses there's too much, and he sends word through the camp: no one make anything more. the people were held back from giving.

original.note: Hebrew: dwelling place, from shakan, to dwell or settle. the tent where God's glory came to rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: chapters of boring building instructions.
what it means: a whole people bringing what they had, so that God could dwell in the middle of the camp.
what a scholar hears: mishkan, from shakan, to dwell; John 1:14's Greek eskenosen means he pitched his tent, and Catholic churches keep a tabernacle.

sources.quoted: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us

notes: Bezalel 'among the first people the Bible says God filled with his Spirit' (31:3; 35:31): Pharaoh earlier describes Joseph as a man in whom is the spirit of God (Genesis 41:38). Hedged with 'among the first'; confirm.
Women's bronze mirrors for the laver (38:8): confirm.
Tabernacle and sanctuary lamp: CCC 1379; Code of Canon Law 938–940 (lamp). Confirm.
John 1:14 Greek eskenosen ('pitched his tent'): standard; confirm.
